messages:
Evelyn S.: Hey team — customer Jess reports a spike of 429s last night during a scheduled data import. They say it happened when the importer spun up ~200 workers from a cloud provider and all used the same API key but came from a pool of ephemeral NAT IPs. They’re confused whether the limit tripped on the org, project, API key, or per-IP bucket. Can infra confirm which quota would have applied and whether the shared key across projects would cause this?

Jess (customer): Yep, we saw ~10-15% of requests 429'ing for ~8 minutes starting 23:02 UTC. We use a single API key per product environment and the VM fleet uses ephemeral NAT IPs. We expected per-key bursting to allow this short spike. :worried:

Pranav G.: Got it — I pulled logs for Jess’s key (key id ends with -jq3). Quick notes: lots of concurrent connections from many IPs; tokens/sec spiked ~x20 above baseline. I see the rate limiter emitted entries: "limit_enforced=project_key_token" and also some "ip_bucket_full" warnings. So both per-key and per-ip paths were involved.

Samira - infra: Adding details on implementation — precedence is: 1) API key soft limits (per-key token/sec + burst window), 2) project-level quotas (aggregate across keys), 3) org-level contractual hard limits, and 4) per-IP protections (to protect edges from single-IP flood). However when a request arrives we evaluate all scopes and the most restrictive active bucket will reject the request. That means if the NAT pool exhausted the per-IP ephemeral bucket, you can still get 429s even if the key’s per-key bucket has capacity.

Evelyn S.: Important: Jess’s traffic pattern hit many distinct IPs within a short epoch — the per-IP protection is implemented as a sliding window keyed by source IP and an overall per-NAT-range fallback. If the cloud provider reuses IPs across other customers, our IP heuristic may have detected noisy neighbor behavior and tightened the IP bucket.

Jess (customer): Is the per-NAT behavior new? We haven't changed anything on our side. Our provider says the pool was stable. If the per-IP rule is the culprit, can you whitelist our IP range?

Samira - infra: We don’t generally whitelist public provider IP ranges because that weakens DDoS protections. But we can do two things: 1) recommend issuing per-worker API keys (one per VM) so per-key burst gets applied independently, or 2) for enterprise customers we can adjust the project-level burst window or route you to Dedicated capacity which has predictable throughput.

Pranav G.: Repro steps I used locally to recreate behavior: spin up 150 concurrent curl workers with the same key, spread across 20 distinct source IPs (I used a proxy farm). Commands: 

```bash
# example, replace KEY and PROXY
for i in {1..150}; do
  PROXY=$(shuf -n1 proxies.txt)
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer KEY" --proxy $PROXY https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate &
done
wait
```

When proxies emulate ephemeral NATs I saw a mix of "project_key_token_rate" and "ip_bucket_full" 429s.

Evelyn S.: From support side, I captured the first 429s and they had error_code: RATE_LIMITED, scope: "ip" in the response body for many samples; others show scope: "project_key". So it's consistent with infra logs. I'm attaching the sample error bodies below: 

```json
{"error":"rate_limited","scope":"ip","retry_after":2}
{"error":"rate_limited","scope":"project_key","retry_after":10}
```

Pranav G.: Root cause summary: the customer's single shared key plus many ephemeral IPs caused both per-key and per-ip buckets to be exercised. Because some IPs hit their per-IP threshold quickly, some requests got ip-scoped 429s even though project/key buckets still had headroom. Also, because their key is used in multiple projects/environments, the project-level aggregate counted toward the project quota and contributed to rejections.

Jess (customer): Oof. So what's the minimal change to avoid this? We can't re-architect our importer quickly.

Samira - infra: Short-term mitigations: 
- Split traffic across multiple API keys (we can issue additional keys) and rotate them across workers.
- Stagger ramp-up (smaller concurrency bursts) so per-IP sliding windows don't fill simultaneously.
- If you can provide a stable egress IP range (static), request support to create a temporary exception or route to Dedicated.

Pranav G.: Also check that the header "X-Forwarded-For" from the customer's proxy isn't masking the true client IP — if the proxy sets a common XFF we might attribute traffic to one IP and trigger stricter limits.

Evelyn S.: Billing note — billing-bot shows they didn't exceed monthly committed units, it’s purely throttling, not billing block. I flagged the ticket so we don't accidentally bill for a retried burst.

billing-bot: Customer account jess-corp has usage spike flagged at 2026-11-12T23:02:11Z, but under contract limit. No billing overage.

Jess (customer): Can you issue a few temp keys and advise on throttling config? We can try splitting across keys and throttling locally.

Evelyn S.: On it — Pranav, can you create 5 short-lived API keys under Jess’s project and tag them "import-surge-1..5"? We'll also provide a recommended client-side backoff snippet.

Pranav G.: Will do. Also leaving this note for product — we should make scoping clearer in the dashboard (show which scope is currently limiting live requests). Logged: https://app.redwood.ai/issue/RED-3812 (product)

Samira - infra: For the backoff recommendation: exponential jittered backoff, cap at 30s, and prefer retrying on project_key scope, but on ip scope prefer linear slow-down since IP issues indicate shared edge congestion. Example snippet: 

```python
# jittered exponential backoff
import random, time
base=0.5
for attempt in range(6):
    wait = min(30, base * (2**attempt)) * random.uniform(0.8,1.2)
    time.sleep(wait)
    retry_request()
```

Evelyn S.: Thanks everyone. I’ll send the temp keys and suggested code to Jess and keep this thread open until they confirm the import succeeds without 429s. :thumbsup:

Jess (customer): Thanks all — appreciate the quick triage. Will report back after the next run. :pray:
